_comment: Real-world systems and their storage choices. Benchmark numbers are vendor-self-reported unless noted. Edited by the nightly maintenance job - keep 'why' paragraphs grounded in cited sources.

systems.name: Claude Code
systems.whyHtml:
Entirely file-based: a hierarchy of CLAUDE.md instruction files loaded at session start, plus an auto-memory directory where the agent writes its own notes - a small always-loaded MEMORY.md index pointing at topic files read on demand.

Why files: the team tried embedding-based retrieval and found agentic search - grep plus reading files in logical order - worked better for code. Files are transparent (users can read and edit the agent's memory), git-versioned, and need zero infrastructure. The bet: for single-project scope with a capable model, retrieval intelligence can live in the agent instead of an index.

systems.name: Letta (MemGPT)
systems.tagline: The agent as its own memory manager
systems.whyHtml:
The MemGPT paper's OS metaphor, productized: labeled, size-limited memory blocks (e.g. persona, human) live inside the context window and the agent edits them with tools; overflow history and archival memories live in Postgres with pgvector for similarity search. Background “sleep-time agents” rewrite the blocks between conversations.

Why this split: the most valuable memories should always be in attention, not fetched - so make the agent responsible for curating that scarce space itself, and page everything else to disk like virtual memory.

systems.name: Mem0
systems.whyHtml:
A two-phase pipeline: an LLM extracts candidate facts from each exchange, then an update gate retrieves similar existing memories and decides ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NOOP - maintenance fused into the write path. Facts land in a vector store; an optional graph layer captures entity relationships.

Why vectors-first: multi-user products need paraphrase-tolerant recall at scale with tight latency budgets. Their paper reports ~90% token savings and 91% lower p95 latency versus stuffing full history into context - the economic argument for extraction over transcripts.

systems.name: Zep / Graphiti
systems.whyHtml:
A bi-temporal knowledge graph: episode nodes (raw messages) feed an entity-and-fact layer, with community summaries above. Every fact edge records when it became true and when the system learned it; contradictions invalidate edges rather than delete them. Retrieval fuses embedding similarity, BM25, and graph traversal.

Why a graph: facts change. A flat vector store can't cleanly answer “what's true now?” versus “what did we believe in June?” - a temporal graph makes both first-class queries, and preserves history losslessly while doing it.

systems.name: ChatGPT memory
systems.whyHtml:
No retrieval at question time at all: user metadata, saved facts, and rolling summaries of recent chats are preloaded into every conversation's context. The 2026 “dreaming” update moved curation offline - a background process periodically re-reads chat history and rewrites a self-updating memory state, revising stale facts on its own.

Why preload + offline synthesis: at consumer scale, per-message retrieval latency is intolerable and users won't curate memory by hand. Spend compute overnight, keep conversations instant - literally reflection during sleep.

systems.name: Hindsight
systems.whyHtml:
An open-source memory bank split into four networks - world facts, experiences, opinions with confidence scores, and entity summaries - with three operations: retain, recall, reflect. Retrieval runs four strategies in parallel (semantic, BM25, graph traversal, temporal) and reranks the union.

Why the split: a memory system that can't distinguish “Maya said X” from “X is true” from “I concluded X” will eventually state beliefs as facts. First system reported past 90% on LongMemEval (self-reported, like most scores in this field).
